title: Pathophysiology: Fluid Compartments & Volume Regulation—Movement, Edema and Perfusion
html:
Fluid balance is more than the amount of water in the body. Safe interpretation asks three linked questions: Where is the fluid, how concentrated is it, and is the circulating volume adequate to perfuse organs? A client can have generalized edema yet inadequate effective circulating volume, or lose free water without losing sodium in the same proportion. The RN therefore clusters history, examination findings, intake and output, daily weight, laboratory trends, and response to treatment rather than labeling volume status from one cue.

Learning goals

  • Distinguish intracellular, interstitial, intravascular, and transcellular fluid.
  • Explain osmosis, tonicity, hydrostatic pressure, oncotic pressure, and lymphatic drainage.
  • Describe how thirst, antidiuretic hormone, RAAS, aldosterone, and natriuretic peptides regulate water and sodium.
  • Differentiate water balance, extracellular volume, and effective circulating volume.
  • Recognize patterns of volume deficit, volume excess, edema, and third spacing.
  • Use weight, intake and output, urine characteristics, vital-sign trends, perfusion, and respiratory findings together.
  • Prioritize respiratory compromise and shock while evaluating response to prescribed therapy.

Body water occupies connected compartments

Intracellular fluid is inside cells and contains most total body water. Extracellular fluid is outside cells and includes interstitial fluid between cells, intravascular plasma, and smaller transcellular collections such as cerebrospinal, pleural, synovial, and gastrointestinal fluid. The proportions vary with age, body composition, and illness, so simple textbook percentages are estimates rather than bedside measurements.

Water crosses cell membranes readily and moves toward the compartment with the greater concentration of effective solute. Sodium and its accompanying anions are major determinants of extracellular tonicity; potassium is the major intracellular cation. Cell size changes when effective extracellular tonicity changes. This is different from merely adding or removing isotonic extracellular fluid, which primarily changes extracellular volume.

Osmolality and tonicity answer different questions

Osmolality describes the number of dissolved particles per kilogram of water. Tonicity describes the effect of nonpenetrating solutes on water movement across cell membranes. A measured serum sodium is therefore interpreted mainly as a water-to-sodium relationship, not a direct inventory of total-body sodium or circulating volume.

Sodium concentration does not reveal volume status by itself
A client with hyponatremia may be volume depleted, near-normal in extracellular volume, or fluid overloaded. A client with hypernatremia may also have different volume states. Assessment must combine concentration with history, perfusion, edema, urine data, weight, and the disease process.

Capillary forces determine interstitial movement

Capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid outward. Plasma oncotic pressure, generated largely by proteins, favors retention of water within the vascular space. Capillary permeability determines how easily fluid and proteins cross, while lymphatic vessels return filtered fluid and protein to the circulation. Edema develops when filtration exceeds lymphatic return.

Mechanisms include increased hydrostatic pressure, reduced plasma oncotic pressure, increased capillary permeability, sodium and water retention, and lymphatic obstruction. Heart failure may raise venous hydrostatic pressure; severe liver disease or protein loss may reduce oncotic pressure; inflammation or burns may increase permeability; lymphatic damage may impair return. The visible swelling can look similar even though the mechanisms and treatment priorities differ.

Third spacing can hide intravascular depletion

Third spacing is a clinical term for fluid sequestered where it does not effectively support circulation, such as marked interstitial edema, ascites, or fluid trapped in injured tissues. Total body water may be increased while effective circulating volume is reduced. Edema therefore does not prove that the circulation is adequately filled.

A client with ascites may also have dizziness, tachycardia, reduced urine output, cool extremities, or worsening kidney function. These cues require prompt evaluation of perfusion and the underlying mechanism; they do not justify independently giving or withholding fluid.

The kidneys and hormones defend balance

Thirst promotes intake when effective osmolality rises and can also respond to reduced circulating volume. Antidiuretic hormone, also called vasopressin, increases renal water reabsorption and concentrates urine. Pain, nausea, stress, medications, and disease can alter ADH release, so urine concentration must be interpreted in context.

Reduced renal perfusion, reduced sodium delivery to the nephron, or sympathetic activation can stimulate renin. The renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system supports vascular tone and sodium retention. Angiotensin II promotes vasoconstriction, thirst, ADH release, and aldosterone secretion. Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion in the distal nephron; water tends to follow retained sodium when available.

Natriuretic peptides are released with cardiac chamber stretch and generally promote sodium excretion and counter-regulatory effects. These systems overlap. Heart, kidney, liver, endocrine, and medication effects can make an apparently appropriate compensatory response maladaptive over time.

Volume deficit threatens perfusion

Extracellular volume deficit can result from hemorrhage, gastrointestinal loss, renal loss, skin loss, inadequate intake, or sequestration outside the effective circulation. Early compensation may preserve blood pressure through tachycardia and vasoconstriction. Concerning trends include increasing thirst, dry mucous membranes, postural symptoms, tachycardia, narrowing pulse pressure, weak pulses, cool extremities, delayed capillary refill, declining urine output, altered mentation, rising respiratory rate, and worsening kidney markers.

No single sign is sufficiently sensitive or specific. Skin turgor varies with age and tissue condition; urine output is altered by kidney function and medications; tachycardia has many causes; blood pressure can remain normal until compensation fails. Hemorrhage can also lower hemoglobin only after fluid shifts, so a normal early value does not exclude acute blood loss.

Perfusion outranks the intake-and-output total
New confusion, hypotension, cool mottled skin, chest discomfort, severe weakness, or falling urine output may signal inadequate organ perfusion. Assess ABCs, obtain help, identify ongoing loss, and follow the emergency pathway rather than waiting for the end-of-shift balance calculation.

Volume excess increases congestion

Extracellular volume excess commonly reflects impaired sodium and water excretion, excessive administration, or disease-associated retention. Findings may include rapid weight gain, dependent or sacral edema, ascites, elevated venous pressure, bounding pulses, hypertension, dyspnea, orthopnea, declining oxygenation, and pulmonary crackles. Pulmonary congestion and increased work of breathing are higher priorities than peripheral swelling alone.

Edema distribution matters. Unilateral painful swelling suggests a different process from symmetric dependent edema. Local inflammation, venous obstruction, or lymphatic dysfunction may cause regional swelling without generalized volume excess. The RN reports the pattern and associated respiratory, vascular, skin, and perfusion findings rather than assuming all edema has one cause.

Measure trends with consistent methods

Daily weight is often the most useful noninvasive trend for fluid gain or loss when measured on the same scale, at the same time, in similar clothing, and with comparable equipment. Roughly 1 liter of retained or lost water changes weight by about 1 kilogram, but body composition and measurement conditions can confound short-term comparisons.

Intake includes oral, enteral, intravenous, and other ordered sources. Output may include urine, drains, emesis, liquid stool, and other measurable losses. Insensible losses through skin and respiration are not captured in a simple total and can increase with fever, tachypnea, burns, or environmental exposure. Record actual measurements and note estimation limits.

Review the time interval, orders, fluid sources, medication effects, urine concentration, kidney function, electrolytes, osmolality when available, hematocrit and protein trends, and the clinical examination. Laboratory concentration can change because water changed, solute changed, or both. A value that appears diluted or concentrated is a clue—not a complete volume assessment.

Fluid therapy changes compartments and carries risk

Prescribed isotonic crystalloid primarily expands extracellular fluid initially, but distribution between plasma and interstitium continues. Hypotonic solutions provide proportionally more free water and can promote cellular swelling. Hypertonic solutions draw water toward the extracellular space and require close monitoring. The ordered fluid, rate, route, indication, comorbidities, and laboratory trend determine safety.

Before and during therapy, assess lung sounds, respiratory effort, oxygenation, perfusion, blood pressure, edema, urine output, weight trend, IV site, and relevant laboratory results. Older adults and clients with cardiac, kidney, or liver dysfunction may tolerate rapid volume changes poorly. Never select or change IV fluid solely from a memorized tonicity label.

Translate fluid balance into clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Identify losses and gains, thirst and access to water, medications, comorbidities, weight change, vital signs, respiratory findings, edema, perfusion, urine output, and laboratory trends.
  2. Analyze cues: Separate water concentration, extracellular volume, effective circulating volume, and regional fluid distribution.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Decide whether respiratory compromise, shock, active loss, impaired excretion, capillary leak, or another mechanism poses the immediate threat.
  4. Generate solutions: Plan monitoring, loss control, prescribed replacement or removal, respiratory support, skin protection, medication review, and escalation.
  5. Take action: Stabilize ABCs, obtain accurate measurements, implement ordered therapy safely, and communicate the mechanism and trend.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Reassess breathing, oxygenation, perfusion, mentation, urine output, weight, edema, laboratory trends, and adverse effects.

Clinical example

A client with cirrhosis and ascites develops dizziness, tachycardia, cool extremities, and decreasing urine output. The abdomen and legs contain excess interstitial or transcellular fluid, but the perfusion pattern suggests reduced effective circulating volume. The RN does not assume that visible edema means adequate intravascular volume. The RN assesses ABCs and perfusion, verifies weight and intake-output trends, reviews current therapy and laboratory data, reports the acute change, follows prescribed management, and evaluates both respiratory congestion and organ perfusion.
